# Order Platform — Service Architecture (rev 4)

## Services

**orders** — owns checkout. On `POST /orders` it calls `inventory.reserve()`
synchronously to hold stock, then calls `billing.charge()` synchronously, then
writes the order row.

**inventory** — owns stock levels. On every reservation it calls
`orders.get_order_context()` to look up the customer's tier and prior order
history so it can apply per-tier stock caps. On restock it calls
`billing.get_open_invoices()` to decide whether to release held stock.

**billing** — owns invoices and payment capture. On charge it calls
`orders.get_line_items()` to price the basket, and calls
`inventory.confirm_reservation()` to mark stock as sold before capture.

## Data

All three services connect to the same Postgres instance (`platform_db`) with
the same application role. `orders`, `inventory`, and `billing` each read and
write the `orders`, `stock_ledger`, and `invoices` tables directly — for
example `billing` updates `stock_ledger.status` at capture time, and
`inventory` updates `orders.state` when a reservation expires.

Schema changes are applied by whichever service ships first; the other two
pick them up on their next deploy.

## Calls

All inter-service calls are blocking HTTP over the cluster network. Default
client timeout is 60s, no retry budget, no circuit breaker. A request thread
in `orders` stays occupied for the whole downstream chain.

## Deployment

One shared Kubernetes namespace, one replica each, deployed together from a
single pipeline. A failing readiness probe on any of the three holds the whole
rollout.

## Open questions

- Should the shared `platform_db` move to a bigger instance class?
- Do we need a second replica of `orders` for the Black Friday window?
